Differences between regular and Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI): • Signals are not correlated (multiplied and averaged) in real time • Collected data is timestamped using atomic clocks or radio timing signals • Data sent later (by internet or hard drive) to correlator at one location • Excellent to detect very compact, bright objects What is e-VLBI? Example: the European VLBI Network (EVN) • Signals are sent and correlated in real time (same for “regular” interferometry) • Different types of radio interferometry not very different in the end (mostly due to data collection and calibration methods) European VLBI Network (EVN) – max baseline 10000 km 29 Event Horizon telescope • One of the World’s largest Interferometers (maximum baseline: 10700 km) • Combines many different telescope facilities from across the world (including ALMA) • Wavelength of observation: 1.3mm and recently 0.87mm • Can therefore achieve a resolution (image detail) of 0.000019 arcseconds • Technique is VLBI: data is stored on disks and shipped to supercomputers at MIT and Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy in Germany 30 Black hole at Centre of M87 • EHT observed supermassive black hole at the centre of M87 (also called M87*) • Resolved close to the radius of the Event Horizon, also called the Schwarzschild radius (the radius relating to the escape velocity for light): 𝑟𝑠 = 2𝐺𝑀 𝑐2 • The mass of M87* is 6.5 billion solar masses(!) • Therefore, 𝑟𝑠 =128 au (au = Earth-Sun distance) • We can find the size of the “Schwarzschild diameter” on the sky using: 𝜃 𝑎𝑟𝑐𝑠𝑒𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑑 𝑜𝑟 ′′ = 𝐷 𝑎𝑢 𝑑 𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑠𝑒𝑐 = 0.000015 ′′ or 15 𝜇𝑎𝑠 Where 𝜃 is the size on the sky, 𝐷 is the physical size and 𝑑 is the distance 31 M87* • EHT results were announced in 2019 • polarisation of emission in M87* and Sgr A* was measured and modelled to determine: • the angular momentum of the black hole • that the magnetic field is dynamically important 33 Comparison with
